title: No comparison in art: Ellington versus Lunceford and Duke's skill at agitating
summary: Jones agrees there should be no ranking of great bands, recalls arguing Duke versus Lunceford, and says Duke knew how to agitate his men.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: He believed that in art there should not be comparison.

No, no. I agree with him totally on that. Because after all, in the final analysis I think that all of these guys are first class, you know, and after you get up in a certain area, it's a matter of choice, you know, a
matter of who you like the best, you know?

And that's philosophical after that, you know, it's not factual necessarily, you know? Like the great Jimmy Lunceford Orchestra was quite an organization, you know? And in my early days I used to argue about Ellington and tell the guys that Duke was the greatest, Duke was the greatest this, that and the other, but then other guys would argue right with me that Lunceford was the greatest. And I hear some of the new things that Capitol and Time-Life put out on Lunceford, and they've got the guys around here right now that can play and write just like they did in those days, and they sound good. Still. Time is a great thing, you know?

If it can hold up with time, you know? So -- but getting back to the question you asked me, as far as Duke doing these things with the men, he was very perceptive. If he could see a bad mood coming, he knew how to agitate.
